Subject: Severe 5xx/429 spike — API errors at peak

Evelyn —

We hit a hard failure this morning during our 11:00 PT batch window. Starting ~10:55 PT we saw elevated 5xx (502/503) and 429 bursts for ~18 minutes, followed by a client retry storm that prolonged the impact. Our team traced the primary errors to timeouts from Redwood endpoints and a sudden queueing/backpressure. We are on a Dedicated pool (D-42 / us-west) and have been using the r-5x.

Impact:
- ~40% of requests returned 5xx during the window
- Many of our callers observed repeated 429s after retries (retry headers show repeat failures)
- Latency spiked from median 120ms to 2.8s at peak

We've attached a short sample of request traces and error lines (error-sample.log). Can you confirm whether Redwood observed any autoscaler failures, GPU OOMs, or notable pod churn in D-42? We need immediate remediation — our org is paying for Dedicated and this is a production outage for multiple customers.

Please escalate to SRE and share a point of contact for faster comms (phone/Slack).

— Aaron Lim

Quick triage notes (observed in the last 24m):
- We saw D-42 nodes hit sustained GPU memory pressure and high context-switching on the runtime processes starting ~10:52 PT. Several inference pods entered CrashLoopBackOff and a subset stayed in Pending as the autoscaler attempted to provision nodes.
- Autoscaler logs show a delayed scale-up: scale-up evaluated at 10:55, but node provisioning and kube-scheduler binding finished ~11:02 due to cloud provisioning cold-starts. That ~7 min lag is where backpressure accumulated.
- The client retry pattern (Helium's 2xx->5xx->retry aggressive loop) amplified queue depth and caused token KV-cache thrashing.

Immediate mitigations applied (11:10 PT):
- Added 4 temporary GPU nodes to D-42 and forced new pods (cordon/uncordon + rollout).
- Enabled a conservative circuit-breaker on D-42 routing: requests with >3 consecutive failures are routed to our hosted fallback pool in us-east.
- Reduced per-request concurrent per-pod worker threads to reduce memory spikes while we stabilize.

Next steps / asks:
- Recommend we temporarily lower the autoscaler threshold and enable a faster scale-up policy for Dedicated pools with predictable high variance workloads (proposal linked).
- Engineering (Markus) to confirm cache-warming strategy when new nodes are added to avoid cold-KV penalties.

Attachments: monitoring-graphs-us-west.png (contains GPU utilization + pod events)
Runbook ref: https://redwood.internal/runbooks/dedicated-saturation

— Sean Gallagher
Senior SRE, Redwood Inference

Thanks Sean — good quick triage. A few engineering notes and an operational fallback plan: 

- Root cause (preliminary): Dedicated pool D-42 experienced a combination of sudden input-rate burst + suboptimal autoscaler cold-start behavior. New instance pool boot times (image pull + CUDA + model warmup) are non-trivial; until the runtime warms the KV cache, per-token cost and memory pressure rise which increases timeouts.

- Immediate fallback I recommend (to be actioned in <30m once authorized):
  1) Route a percentage (start 20%) of inbound traffic for a 30-minute window to the hosted us-east pool while we finish node provisioning in us-west. This reduces peak load on D-42 and buys time for cache-warm.
  2) Enable temporary aggressive rate-limiting on new client sessions coming into D-42 (soft throttle) to avoid retry storms.
  3) Post-incident: tune autoscaler to be more sensitive to queue depth and add pre-warm warm-up instances for known high-variance accounts.

Cost / executive note: routing to hosted pools and adding immediate burst nodes increases spend in the short window; recommend approval for a temporary burst budget (~$8-12k) charged to account-level system/EmergencyOps.

If we get a rapid approval, I can put the routing rule in place and help with cache-warm scripts.

— Markus Klein
VP, Inference Engine
